name: Effect of External Thermo-Convective Perturbation on Cool Flame Dynamics: A Multidimensional Multi-Physics CFD Analysis
study_type: computational (3-D CFD model in OpenFOAM), validated against ISS FLEX flight data from PSI; no new experiments
investigators_note: Citation on the PSI record: Farouk T, Hicks M. Proposal title is the same as the investigation title.
objective: Use FLEX flight data from PSI to quantify how externally imposed thermal and convective perturbations controlled the dynamics and final fate of already established droplet cool flames, and to explain run-to-run variability by separating the roles of deliberate heating and unintended drift-induced convection. For small and large droplets, map stability windows for ignition, sustained oscillation, transition to hot ignition and warm-flame behaviour, and extinction in microgravity, and produce reusable models and sensitivity analyses coupling low-temperature chemistry with transport and radiation.
hypothesis: External thermo-convective perturbations (imposed temperature gradients, non-uniform heating, oscillatory or shear inflow) govern cool-flame ignition, oscillation, transition to hot ignition and extinction by shifting residence time and scalar dissipation. In microgravity, where buoyancy is suppressed, this forcing was expected to dominate transport.
approach: A 3-D CFD model of n-alkane droplet cool flames in microgravity was built in OpenFOAM, coupling variable-density Navier-Stokes flow with low-temperature chemistry, heat and mass transfer, and radiation. After checking the model against ISS FLEX measurements, controlled simulations examined three forcing modes: (i) convection alone, to mimic droplet drift; (ii) imposed heat flux; (iii) convection plus heating, for large (1 to 4 mm) and sub-millimeter (about 0.5 mm) droplets. The work started with simplified chemistry and moved to reduced mechanisms for parameter sweeps over forcing amplitude and frequency, ambient composition (including ozone-assisted cases) and pressure. Ignition delay, oscillation frequency and amplitude, stand-off ratio and extinction diameter were extracted from each case to build stability maps for cool-flame onset, persistence and quenching, which were compared with FLEX observations and used to guide future test matrices.
fuel: n-alkane droplets (specific fuels not named on the record)

space_benefits: Potential to improve spacecraft fire-safety modeling by resolving cool-flame and extinction behaviour in microgravity; uses FLEX data to help define safer operating envelopes and materials.
earth_benefits: Advances understanding of low-temperature combustion relevant to engine knock, efficiency and emissions, and provides validated CFD tools transferable to practical combustors.

data_quality_notes: Ground (computational) investigation: there are no flight or laboratory tests in PSI-117, and no experimental or modeling table on the record.
The description is written as completed work, but the record states no results; findings would be in the dissertation, presentations and analyzed data files, which were not reviewed here.
The record names neither the specific n-alkane fuels nor the ranges of oxygen, pressure, forcing amplitude and frequency used.

The 2018 conference paper and the 2019 journal paper titled 'Oscillatory cool flame combustion behavior of submillimeter sized n-alkane droplet under near limit conditions' appear to be the same work at two stages.

Some listed publications (2017) date from the first months of the grant, and some cover sub-millimeter droplet experiments outside the CFD scope described, so the list is the team's related work rather than outputs of this study only.
The investigation ended on 14 February 2022, but the data were submitted on 18 September 2024 and first released on 10 June 2026.
